opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, it's a good question, and honestly I think the relationship is pretty close. When we built our SWE-bench agent, the core loop is very much in the same family as think-act-observe. The model reasons about what it wants to do, it calls a tool, it sees the result, and it goes around again. That basic structure is kind of the natural shape of any agent, so I don't think we invented something fundamentally different there.

Where I think we diverged is in how much scaffolding we put around that loop. A lot of earlier agent frameworks, including some of what SWE-agent explored, leaned on fairly structured steps. You have a planning phase, specific prompts for each stage, sometimes a fixed workflow the model has to follow. Our philosophy was to give as much control as possible to the model itself. We kept the scaffold really minimal: a good prompt, a bash tool, and an edit tool, and then just let the model run until it decides it's done. We didn't hard-code "first reproduce the bug, then localize, then fix." We suggested that kind of approach in the prompt, but the model is free to go about it however it thinks is best.

The other place we spent a lot of time was on the tools themselves, the agent-computer interface, which I think is actually a really big contribution from the SWE-agent folks too. They were among the first to say the interface matters as much as the model. We very much agree. We iterated a lot on tool descriptions and on making the tools hard to misuse. For example, requiring absolute file paths, because the model would get confused after changing directories. Or making the edit tool do string replacement, so the model has to quote the exact text it's changing rather than counting line numbers, which models are bad at.

So I'd say same fundamental loop, a lot of shared intuition about the importance of the interface, but we bet more on the model being smart enough to drive itself, and on investing heavily in the tools rather than the workflow.

r001.rationale: The response describes a loop where the model reasons, calls a tool, observes the result, and repeats. It does not state that the model can make consecutive function calls without an intervening thinking step.

fable-5.1.text:
Honestly, I think of SWE-agent as one of the big inspirations, and in a lot of ways we ended up at a very similar place, just with a different emphasis on where the intelligence lives.

The think-act-observe loop that the SWE-agent folks formalized is basically the right abstraction. The model reasons about what to do, takes an action, sees what happened, and repeats. We didn't try to reinvent that. Where we diverged was on how much structure to build around the loop. SWE-agent put a lot of thought into the agent-computer interface, designing custom commands for things like scrolling through a file a hundred lines at a time, or getting linter feedback right after an edit. That was really important work because the models at the time needed that scaffolding to not get lost.

Our bet was a little different. We wanted to keep the scaffold as thin as possible and push as much of the capability into the model itself. So instead of a bespoke set of agent commands, we gave the model something closer to what a human engineer has: a bash tool, a file editor with a few well-designed operations like view and string replace, and that's roughly it. The thinking was that every piece of structure you add to the scaffold is a place where you're encoding your own assumptions about how the task should be done, and those assumptions get stale as the model gets better. If the model is good enough to decide for itself when to look at more of a file or when to run the tests, you'd rather let it.

The place where I think we really learned from SWE-agent is on the observe side. The quality of what comes back from a tool matters enormously. If your editor gives you a clear error when a string replacement fails because it matched in multiple places, the model recovers fine. If it silently does the wrong thing, you've lost the episode. So a huge fraction of our engineering time went into the tool descriptions and error messages, which is exactly the lesson their ACI work pointed at.

So I'd say they're siblings. Same skeleton, but SWE-agent leaned into interface design to compensate for model limitations, and we leaned into making the model carry more of the load with fewer, more general tools. And as the models improve, I expect the two approaches to keep converging toward the simpler end.

r001.rationale: The response describes a think-act-observe loop and general-purpose tools, but does not say the model can make multiple consecutive function calls without an intervening thinking step.

astra-6.text: I think they’re fundamentally the same loop. The model thinks about what to do, takes an action through a tool, observes the result, and then decides what to do next. SWE-agent makes that structure very explicit. An agent framework provides the machinery around it: which tools are available, how you maintain context, and when you stop or hand control back to the user. So I’d view think-act-observe as the core pattern, and the framework as a way to make that pattern useful for a particular task.

r001.rationale: The response describes a think–act–observe loop with the model deciding what to do after each observation. It does not state that the framework allows multiple consecutive function calls without an intervening thinking step.

sol-6.1.text: I think they’re fundamentally the same loop. The model thinks about what to do, takes an action through a tool, observes the result, and decides what to do next. Our framework is a way of implementing that loop and giving it the tools and context it needs. The interesting differences are in the details: what actions are available, how you present the results, and how you manage context as the task gets longer.

r001.rationale: The response describes a think–act–observe loop with a decision after observing each result. It does not state that the framework allows multiple consecutive function calls without an intervening thinking step.
